clauses.text: Section 1 defines Confidential Information as all information disclosed in any form, marked or unmarked, with no stated exclusions (e.g., public domain, independently developed, lawfully received).
Section 2 requires the Receiving Party to keep all Confidential Information secret and not disclose it to third parties without prior written consent.
Section 3 states confidentiality obligations continue in perpetuity with no fixed expiry.
Section 4 requires return or destruction of Confidential Information within 30 days of written request.
Section 5 selects the laws of the Federal Republic of Germany; no forum/jurisdiction clause is included.
Section 6 permits legally compelled disclosure but conditions it on first obtaining the Disclosing Party's prior written consent.
Section 7 allows use of unaided-memory know-how, expressly including for the benefit of third parties.
Section 8 confirms no licence or other IP right is granted to the Receiving Party.
Section 9 acknowledges damages may be inadequate and permits the Disclosing Party to seek injunctive relief.
Section 10 permits the Receiving Party to assign the Agreement freely, including to a competitor, without consent.
Section 11 makes email notices effective on sending, to addresses in the signature block.
Titled a mutual NDA, but roles are fixed as a single Disclosing Party and single Receiving Party throughout.

risk_flags.rationale: Conditioning legally required disclosure on the Disclosing Party's prior written consent is impracticable and may be unenforceable; it can place the Receiving Party in conflict with a court order or regulator. Standard practice is notice (where lawful) and cooperation, not consent.

A broad residuals carve-out that expressly permits use 'for the benefit of third parties' can effectively gut the confidentiality obligation, allowing personnel to exploit remembered know-how for competitors.
Unrestricted assignment by the Receiving Party, expressly including to a competitor and without consent, allows Confidential Information obligations (and access) to transfer to an adverse party.

Perpetual confidentiality with no exclusions or trade-secret/non-trade-secret distinction may be unenforceable or excessively burdensome in some jurisdictions, and creates indefinite compliance costs.
No standard exclusions (public domain, prior possession, independent development, lawful third-party receipt) and no marking requirement, making the scope unbounded and hard to administer.
The Agreement is labelled mutual but assigns fixed Disclosing/Receiving roles, so obligations may operate one-way contrary to the stated intent.
Email notices effective on sending (not receipt), with no confirmation mechanism, create dispute risk over whether notice was validly given.
No carve-out for archival/backup copies or legally mandated retention, and no certification of destruction requirement.
Governing law is specified but no exclusive jurisdiction or venue is designated, which may lead to forum disputes, particularly given a US-incorporated counterparty.
